title: Big Data applied to criminal investigations: expectations of professionals of police cooperation in the European Union
thesis: Explores expectations of EU police cooperation professionals regarding Big Data in criminal investigations using DNA databases, highlighting perceived benefits (cold cases, interoperability) and risks (genetic discrimination, privacy).
theme_1_justification: Not addressed. The paper discusses data interoperability and sharing within law enforcement but does not engage with dual-use or technology transfer between civilian and military domains.
theme_2_justification: Tangential mention. The paper discusses algorithmic bias and risks of 'bad profiling' (p. 1173) and concerns about inaccurate predictions, but does not deeply engage with epistemic authority, black-boxing, or democratic deliberation.
theme_3_justification: Not addressed. The paper focuses on criminal investigations and police cooperation, not on the city as a programmable system or modulation of urban populations.
theme_4_justification: Not addressed. No discussion of spatial destruction, urbicide, home unmaking, or weaponisation of civilian infrastructure.
key_quotes: I think this project [Big Data] is worked in EUROPOL, according to what I heard. They are doing something like this [Big Data], to connect all the information from the police which is about criminal acts (...) I think this is an analytical weapon (...) to connect all of this information and to put it into some sort of sheet, it is now an analytical sheet, just to complete also with forensic, biological and photography, fingerprint, DNA. And this [Big Data] could be very helpful in these cases.

This is an ethical question. The [Big Data] analysis, we could have bad profiling. We do not want bad profiling. Because you could find that people with certain loci are more criminals, there are more criminals in a certain… But this correlation could not be a real correlation. (...) My opinion is that we have to analyse those kind of connections, but we could be very careful with this.

Well, if I have something to hide, I would not want it [Big Data]. But being the normal law-abiding citizen, I do not have any problem with that. I cannot see anyone having any problem unless you have something to hide. (...) So, OK, maybe my privacy is not going to be as private, but if something happens to my property, thanks to the system it [Big Data] can help me, for example, to apprehend the suspect or perpetrator.
policy_relevance: Highlights the need for regulation and data protection frameworks for Big Data in criminal investigations, and calls for anticipatory governance to address transparency, accountability, and public trust.
